It originated in an application (no. 22410/93) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25. The applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and sought leave to present their own case. The applicants’ neighbours, Mr and Mrs T., instituted proceedings seeking damages for problems experienced with their sewerage. On 1 May 1991, Judge Clarke gave judgment against the applicants. Their appeal was subsequently dismissed by the Court of Appeal. On 25 April 1997 the Chamber decided to dispense with a hearing in the case. The Government, applicants and Commission were invited to submit written comments on the matters raised in the memorials. The applicants applied for legal aid in November 1991. A delay of nine months was caused because of a misapprehension in this respect. The judge ordered that 4,599 pounds sterling (GBP) should be paid to Mr and Mrs T. forthwith and that the applicants should in addition pay them GBP 6,000 in instalments of GBP 100 per month. The applicants sought legal aid to appeal against this decision. The applicants were requested to lodge the relevant documents by 2 May 1994. Extensions of this time-limit were granted on 25 April, 24 May, 16 June, 6 July and again on 27 July 1994 at the request of the applicants. It later transpired that Judge Clarke’s notes had been either lost or did not exist. On 6 October 1994, the registrar granted the applicants’ request that transcripts of the judgment of Judge Darwall-Smith be produced at public expense. On 29 March 1995 the application was listed for hearing. After the hearing on 19 June 1995, the Court of Appeal confirmed Judge Dar wall Smith's judgment of 13 November 1992 and dismissed the appeal.

text: The case was referred to the Court on 12 July 1993 by the European Commission of Human Rights. It originated in an application (no. 18949/91) against the United Kingdom lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 25 March 1991 by a British citizen. The object of the request and the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations. The applicant, Mr Peter Maxwell, is a British citizen born in 1944. On 14 or 15 February 1990 two masked men broke into a private house, situated in Stevenston, Scotland. They assaulted the occupant causing him severe injury and permanent disfigurement. On 19 February 1990 Mr Maxwell was arrested together with another man. They were indicted on a charge of assault. Both held in custody until trial started on 28 May 1990 in the High Court of Justiciary at Kilmarnock. On 29 May 1990 the jury found the applicant guilty of the charge. Taking account of his bad criminal record, the judge sentenced him to five years' imprisonment. The applicant lodged with the court a note of appeal setting out grounds which he formulated himself. The grounds of appeal can be summarised as follows: (a) the applicant had not been able to substantiate his contention that a crucial witness was giving false evidence against him because to do so would have involved revealing to the jury a previous conviction; (b) a number of witnesses had not be called by the Crown or by the Defence; (c) crucial evidence had been entirely fabricated; (d) the verdict of the jury was not supported by the evidence. On 25 January 1991, the Board informed Mr Maxwell that his application had been refused as the Board was not satisfied, as it was required to be under the relevant legislation. His solicitors advised him that he should abandon his appeal but he chose not to accept their advice. The applicant decided to proceed with his appeal personally. The Crown was represented by counsel but there is no indication that he intervened at the hearing. On the same date the court dismissed the appeal.

text: The case originated in an application (no. 75252/01) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Five Swedish nationals, Mr Tommy Evaldsson, Mr Johan Svahn, Mr Tonnie Hodell, Mr Jonny Lindqvist and Mr Conny Brandt (“the applicants”), and the Swedish Construction Industries (Sveriges Byggindustrier) (hereinafter “the Industries”) on 4 September 2001. The applicants alleged that the levying of monitoring fees on the individual applicants’ wages involved violations of Articles 9, 10, 11 and 14. The case involved the Swedish Building Workers’ Union (Svenska Byggnadsarbetareförbundet, hereinafter “the Union’) and the Industries. The relevant local branch of the Union in the instant case was the Stockholm branch, Byggettan. If inspections were carried out in accordance with the collective agreement, the local branch had the right to reimbursement of the costs involved on the basis of a fee of 1.5%. Two of the applicants, Mr Evaldsson and Mr Hodell, were heard by the Labour Court. They submitted that they opposed the deductions because they did not think that the monitoring work was of any use to them and considered the deductions an unnecessary expense. Allegedly, they felt that the deductions were unjust. Company complied with their requests, stopped paying the fees to Byggettan and did not provide it with the above-mentioned wage information. Union claimed that a ban on the levying of monitoring fees on unorganised workers’ wages would violate the positive rights of its members. Byggettan argued that the positive aspect of the freedom of association under Article 11 of the Convention was stronger than its negative counterpart. By a judgment of 7 March 2001, the Labour Court rejected the Industries’ claims. In a case from 1977 (AD 1977 nr 222), the court had found that the monitoring of time-based wages was wholly different from the measuring of piecework. The Labour Court. concluded that the monitoring fee deductions did not entail membership of the Union and that no pressure had been exerted to compel the applicants to join the Union against their will. It found that the fee in issue was deducted in accordance with their employer's obligations under the collective labour agreement, and it was, accordingly, difficult to see a link with the Union’s ideology. Noting that it could appear offensive to an unorganised worker to have to contribute to the work, the court stated that it was not without importance that the un Organised worker in fact obtained something in return. The company had not influenced or forced the applicants to join the Union. The company had been obliged to make a deduction from their wages in accordance with the collective labour agreement. The case was heard in the High Court in London on Wednesday. The jury was told that the company had made the deduction from the applicants' wages. It was also told that it had been in breach of the company's contract of employment.
